item.title: Himure & Akahage Shrines, Bungo-ono — Guide
item.description: In the rural inland region of Bungo-ono in Oita, small local shrines set amid forest, rock and countryside offer a peaceful, authentic experience of rural Shinto worship away from the crowds. Bungo-ono is a landscape shaped by ancient volcanic activity from nearby Mount Aso, giving it dramatic gorges, waterfalls, rock formations and rich soil — a designated UNESCO Global Geopark. Its shrines, often tucked into atmospheric natural settings among old trees, mossy stone and streams, reflect the deep-rooted local connection between the community, the land and its deities.

item.title: Kushida Shrine: The Heart of Old Hakata — Guide
item.description: Kushida Shrine is the tutelary shrine of the old merchant district of Hakata and one of the most beloved shrines in Fukuoka. Founded over a thousand years ago and affectionately called ‘O-Kushida-san’, it is the spiritual centre of Hakata life and the starting point of the city’s greatest festival, the Hakata Gion Yamakasa. Even outside the July festival, you can see a towering, elaborately decorated kazariyama float on permanent display in the grounds, giving a sense of the festival’s scale year-round.

item.title: Oyamazumi Shrine, Omishima Island — Guide
item.description: Oyamazumi Shrine on Omishima island is one of the most important and atmospheric shrines in western Japan, long revered by warriors as a guardian of soldiers and sailors. For over a thousand years, victorious samurai and commanders dedicated their armour and weapons here in thanks, and as a result the shrine’s treasure house holds an astonishing collection — the greatest concentration of nationally designated armour and swords in Japan, including pieces linked to famous historical figures.

item.title: Takachiho Shrine — Guide
item.description: Takachiho Shrine (Takachiho Jinja), founded some 1,900 years ago, is the spiritual heart of the mythologically rich town of Takachiho in northern Miyazaki. Set in a serene, atmospheric grove of towering ancient cedar trees, the weathered wooden shrine radiates a deep sense of age and sanctity. Among its treasures is a magnificent pair of 800-year-old ‘meoto sugi’ (husband-and-wife cedar trees), joined at the roots, around which couples walk hand in hand for blessings of love, marriage and harmony.

item.title: Tateba Shrine — Guide
item.description: Miyazaki (historically Hyuga) is deeply woven into Japan’s founding mythology as the land from which the legendary first emperor, Emperor Jimmu, is said to have set out on his eastern expedition to found the nation. Small shrines along the coast, such as Tateba Shrine, are tied to these ancient legends, marking places connected to Jimmu and the gods of the creation myths. Atmospheric and steeped in history, such a shrine offers a quiet, contemplative stop away from the busier sights: weathered wooden buildings, a torii gate, a coastal or wooded setting, and a palpable sense of the deep mythological roots that run through this part of Kyushu.

item.title: Tatsuda Shrine — Guide
item.description: Tatsuda Shrine is a serene Shinto shrine in Kumamoto, tucked among woodland and greenery in a quiet setting away from the city bustle. Approached through torii gates and shaded paths, its wooden shrine buildings, mossy stone lanterns and forested grounds create a calm, spiritual atmosphere, especially beautiful in the fresh green of early summer and the coloured leaves of autumn. The Tatsuda area is historically associated with the ruling Hosokawa clan, whose family temple and gardens lie nearby, adding a layer of samurai-era heritage to a visit.

item.title: Usa Shrine (Usa Jingū) — Guide
item.description: Usa Shrine (Usa Jingū), in northern Oita, is the head shrine of the more than 40,000 Hachiman shrines throughout Japan, and one of the country’s most venerable and important Shinto sites. Founded in the eighth century, it enshrines Hachiman, the deified Emperor Ōjin and the deity of war and protection long revered by the imperial court and samurai. Set amid a tranquil precinct of ancient forest, ponds and vermilion bridges, its striking main halls are built in the distinctive ‘Hachiman-zukuri’ architectural style — a designated National Treasure — with brilliant orange-red buildings roofed in cypress bark.

item.title: Hatsumode Guide: Tokyo's New Year Shrine Visits Explained
item.description: Every year, in the first three days of January, Japan undergoes a collective ritual unlike anything in most other countries: over 100 million people visit a shrine or temple. Not individually, over the course of a season — but in three days, as a single national event. In Tokyo alone, Meiji Shrine receives more than 3 million visitors between January 1st and 3rd, making it the most-visited shrine in Japan during hatsumode (初詣) — the first shrine visit of the New Year.

item.title: Meiji Jingu Guide: Tokyo's Forest Shrine in the Heart of Harajuku
item.description: Step through the towering wooden torii at the edge of Harajuku and the city simply vanishes. Within a few paces the neon, the crowds, and the noise of Tokyo’s busiest youth district give way to a deep, hushed forest — 100,000 trees of 365 species, planted a century ago by volunteers from across Japan. At the centre stands Meiji Jingu, the Shinto shrine dedicated to Emperor Meiji and Empress Shoken, and one of the most spiritually significant places in the capital.

item.title: Sumiyoshi Taisha Guide: Osaka's Ancient Shrine & Drum Bridge
item.description: The head shrine of some 2,300 Sumiyoshi shrines across Japan, Sumiyoshi Taisha is one of the country’s oldest and most distinctive Shinto sites — founded in the 3rd century, long before Buddhist influence reached Japan, and built in a rare ancient style found nowhere else. Its image is the steep, vermilion Taiko-bashi (drum bridge) arching over a pond, one of Osaka’s most photographed scenes. Revered as a guardian of sea travel and a bringer of good fortune, it draws over two million worshippers at New Year alone.

item.title: Yamanashi Power Spots: Sacred Shrines at the Foot of Mt Fuji
item.description: Mt Fuji has been an object of religious devotion in Japan for at least 1,300 years. The mountain is worshipped as a kami (divine spirit) by Shinto tradition, considered a manifestation of the Bodhisattva Kannon in Buddhist cosmology, and has drawn ascetic practitioners, pilgrims, and seekers of supernatural energy to its slopes since the Nara period. The shrines and sacred sites clustered at its base in Yamanashi are among the most spiritually charged locations in the country — places where the boundary between the natural world and the divine world has historically been understood to be permeable.
